## New Features

- Follow thread links from search results and transcripts to open saved conversations and nested agents in the terminal. (#62332)
- Press `Tab` to complete arguments for supported slash commands. For example, `/mcp lo` completes to `/mcp login`. (#62343)
- Jump between task groups in the agent command center with `Shift+Up` and `Shift+Down`. (#62200)
- Optional stdio MCP servers with cached tool lists now start on their first tool call by default. (#62366)
- Set an approval reviewer for individual connected app tools in `config.toml`. (#62360)
- App-server clients can select Amazon Bedrock Runtime during setup or sign-in. (#62222)

## Bug Fixes

- `codex exec resume` restores saved sandbox permissions, the working directory, and workspace roots unless explicitly overridden. (#62194)
- Remote sessions preserve working directories, workspace roots, and writable paths when the client and server run on different operating systems. (#62375, #62376, #62377)
- Codex reports provider errors as soon as they arrive in a response stream and identifies which API spend limit was reached. (#62329, #62356)
- Interrupting a parent turn preserves queued replies from child agents for the next turn. (#62348)
- Use `PageUp` and `PageDown` to read and submit answer choices that are taller than the terminal’s answer area. (#62209)
- Cloud replies that finish after history loads now update in place, keeping the terminal transcript in order. (#62403)

## Documentation

- The bundled `openai-docs` skill now covers migration to GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, including endpoint choices and tool-calling requirements. (#62447)

## Chores

- Code Mode now uses gRPC for all host connections. The `code_mode_host_grpc` setting is deprecated. (#62476)
- Python formatting and SDK type generation now verify dependency hashes against the repository lockfile. (#62346)

## Changelog

sources.data: # Models > For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://learn.chatgpt.com/llms.txt). Markdown versions of documentation pages are available by appending `.md` to the page URL. Choosing a model is about finding the right balance of speed, cost, and capability for your task. Sometimes you need a quick first draft. Other times, a complex problem calls for more careful reasoning. This guide introduces our latest models, shows where each one shines, and helps you find a starting point for your work. GPT-5.5 retirement: [See replacement models and migration steps](#gpt-55-retirement). ## Choose a model In Work or Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app, use the model and reasoning control beneath the composer to choose an available model and adjust its reasoning effort. If you see the Power slider, open **Advanced** to choose a specific model, such as GPT-6.2 Astra. **Reasoning effort** guides how much work the model puts into thinking through your request. Higher effort can improve results for complex tasks, but it takes longer and uses more tokens. Start with the default effort and increase it when the task needs deeper planning or analysis. **Ultra** mode goes beyond a single-agent run. It uses [subagents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents) to accelerate complex work, making it useful for larger tasks that can be split across subagents. ## Choose a model These recommendations apply to **ChatGPT Work** on the web. Use the model and reasoning control beneath the composer to choose an available model and adjust its reasoning effort. **Reasoning effort** guides how much work the model puts into thinking through your request. Higher effort can improve results for complex tasks, but it takes longer and uses more tokens. Start with the default effort and increase it when the task needs deeper planning or analysis. **Ultra** mode goes beyond a single-agent run. It uses [subagents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents) to accelerate complex work, making it useful for larger tasks that can be split across subagents. ## Choose a model GPT-6.1 Terra requires Codex CLI 0.159.0 or later. To use it, run `codex -m gpt-6.1-terra`. In an interactive CLI session, use `/model` to switch models or adjust reasoning effort. To start Codex with Sol, use `--model` or its `-m` alias: ```bash codex --model gpt-6.2-sol ``` The same option works with non-interactive runs. For example: ```bash codex exec -m gpt-6.2-sol "Review the current changes" ``` **Reasoning effort** guides how much work the model puts into thinking through your request. Higher effort can improve results for complex tasks, but it takes longer and uses more tokens. Start with the default effort and increase it when the task needs deeper planning or analysis. **Ultra** mode goes beyond a single-agent run. It uses [subagents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents) to accelerate complex work, making it useful for larger tasks that can be split across subagents. ## Choose a model Use the model switcher below the composer to choose an available model and reasoning effort. **Reasoning effort** guides how much work the model puts into thinking through your request. Higher effort can improve results for complex tasks, but it takes longer and uses more tokens. Start with the default effort and increase it when the task needs deeper planning or analysis. **Ultra** mode goes beyond a single-agent run. It uses [subagents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents) to accelerate complex work, making it useful for larger tasks that can be split across subagents. This example shows the Power slider for a ChatGPT Work account with access to both GPT-6.2 models. New Work chats start with GPT-6.2 Sol at **Light** on supported consumer plans or **Medium** in Enterprise workspaces with the model enabled. Move the Power slider toward **Smarter** for deeper reasoning or **Faster** for faster, lower-cost work. Open **Advanced** to choose a specific model or reasoning effort from the options available to your account. ## Recommended models GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol are now available in ChatGPT Work and Codex on [supported plans and clients](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing#feature-availability). For demanding work across code, apps, or research, choose GPT-6.2 Astra. In Codex, try Astra to trace a bug across services, fix it, and test the change. See [Prompting GPT-6.2 in Codex](https://learn.chatgpt.com/guides/prompting-gpt-6-2-astra). Choose GPT-6.2 Sol for everyday coding, writing, and work across several sources. It costs fewer credits per token than GPT-6.2 Astra at [Standard speed](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing#token-rates). GPT-6.1 Terra is a fast, efficient choice for writing, visual understanding, and computer use. Luna suits focused, repeatable tasks. These recommendations apply to ChatGPT Work and Codex. For Chat availability, see [models in ChatGPT](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001354-gpt-6-and-other-models-in-chatgpt) in the Help Center. To use a longer context window in Codex, set `model_context_window` in [`config.toml`](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-advanced#model-reasoning-verbosity-and-limits). GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol each support a context window of up to 1 million tokens. GPT-6.1 Sol uses a default context window of 500,000 tokens in Codex and ChatGPT Work. See [pricing](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/pricing) for subscription usage and credit rates. For model availability, pricing, and usage limits, see [ChatGPT Work and Codex](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001275-chatgpt-work-and-codex) in the Help Center. ## Choosing a model Start with a task you know well and compare the result with what you need. Consider how long you're willing to wait, how much usage the task requires, and the level of detail or judgment involved. You can change models as your work changes. ### Where each model shines - **GPT-6.2 Astra or GPT-6 Astra, for the hardest end-to-end work.** Choose an available Astra model for tasks that need sustained reasoning across code, apps, or research. Give it the sources, constraints, and checks that define a useful result. - **GPT-6.2 Sol, for everyday work.** Choose Sol to edit code, draft documents, or turn several sources into a plan. - **GPT-6.1 Terra, for everyday writing and visual work.** Choose Terra for clear communication, interpreting images and screens, and completing tasks across supported apps. Try it for drafting proposals, reviewing visual materials, or filling out forms from source documents. - **Luna, for clear, repeatable tasks.** Choose Luna for specific, high-volume tasks when you know what a good result looks like, such as extraction, classification, transformation, and structured summaries. ### Try an example Use your own materials with these prompts, and tell ChatGPT what a useful result should include. | Model | Task | Example prompt | | ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | GPT-6.2 Astra or GPT-6 Astra | Work through a complex decision. | "Compare these three vendor proposals against our requirements. Explain the tradeoffs, recommend an option, and list the questions we should resolve before deciding." | | GPT-6.2 Sol | Bring several sources into a working document. | "Use this project brief, meeting notes, and timeline to draft an implementation plan. Identify dependencies, flag conflicting details, and list the decisions we still need to make." | | GPT-6.1 Terra | Make sense of visual information. | "Review these dashboard screenshots and summarize the main changes. Refer to the chart labels and values, and flag anything you can't read confidently." | | Luna | Organize information into a consistent format. | "Turn these meeting notes into a table of action items, owners, and due dates. Mark any missing owner or date as unspecified." | Review the result against your source materials, especially names, numbers, and details taken from images. For tasks on websites or in desktop apps, check the [browser use](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/browser) and [computer use](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/computer-use) setup requirements first. ### Pick a reasoning effort For example, you might use a lower effort to rewrite a short email and a higher effort to compare several proposals with competing requirements. For GPT-6.2 Astra or GPT-6.2 Sol, start with the effort your client selects and adjust it based on the task. For Luna, start with **High**. For GPT-6 Astra, start with **Light** (`low` in configuration). Increase the effort for tasks that need more planning, analysis, or checking. - **Light** in the ChatGPT desktop app, ChatGPT Work on the web, and IDE extension, or **Low** in the CLI, suits quick, well-scoped tasks. - **Medium** balances speed and depth for tasks that need more planning. - **High** and **Extra High** suit difficult work with multiple steps, sources, or tradeoffs. [Learn more in our Model selection guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/model-selection#how-to-think-about-models-and-reasoning-effort) ### Know when to use Max or Ultra **Max** gives the selected model more time to reason about a single task. Use it for the hardest problems, when depth matters more than speed or usage. If you don't see Max in the ChatGPT desktop app, check your app settings. **Ultra** uses [subagents](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents) to handle separate parts of a complex task in parallel. Choose it when you can divide the work into meaningful parts. Most tasks do not need Max or Ultra. GPT-6 Luna supports reasoning efforts up to **Max**, but not **Ultra**. In the CLI, use `/model`, choose a model, then select **More reasoning…** to see its supported Max or Ultra options. If your model supports Ultra but it doesn't appear in the desktop app's model slider, go to **Settings** > **Configuration**, then turn on **Ultra in model picker slider**. ## GPT-5.5 retirement Effective October 14, 2026, at noon PDT (19:00 UTC), GPT-5.5 retires from Codex for users signed in with ChatGPT. The OpenAI API and Codex sessions authenticated with an API key aren't affected. For Codex with ChatGPT sign-in, choose an available replacement: - On Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans, choose **GPT-6.1 Sol** (`gpt-6.1-sol`) when available. - On Free and Go plans, choose **GPT-6 Luna** (`gpt-6-luna`) in the desktop app when available. Replace `gpt-5.5` in workspace defaults, saved model settings, managed configurations, custom agents, scheduled tasks, and scripts that select a model. See [workspace model availability](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/workspace-model-availability#prepare-for-the-gpt-55-retirement) for administrator guidance. ## Other models With API-key authentication, model availability follows your API organization and project. GPT-5.5 remains available through the OpenAI API and in Codex sessions authenticated with an API key. See the [API model catalog](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models). For a custom model provider or gateway, use a compatible Responses API endpoint. See [Custom model providers](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-advanced#custom-model-providers) for configuration and [Gateway compatibility](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/enterprise/gateway-compatibility) for streaming, tool, and conversation requirements. Current Codex releases don't support `wire_api = "chat"` or a Chat Completions-only endpoint. ## Deprecated Codex models GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark retired on September 14, 2026, and is no longer available in the ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, or IDE extension. Update saved configurations, custom agents, and scripts that select `gpt-5.3-codex-spark` to use an [available model](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/models#recommended-models). See the [Spark retirement notice](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/changelog#codex-2026-09-14-codex-spark-deprecation). GPT-5.5 retires from Codex with ChatGPT sign-in on October 14, 2026, at noon PDT (19:00 UTC). Replace `gpt-5.5` with a model available to your account and client. API-key sessions aren't affected. See [GPT-5.5 retirement](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/models#gpt-55-retirement) for plan-specific replacements and the migration checklist. The `gpt-5.4` and `gpt-5.4-mini` models retired from Codex with ChatGPT sign-in on August 31, 2026. Replace `gpt-5.4` with `gpt-6-sol` and `gpt-5.4-mini` with `gpt-6-luna` when available to your plan and client. In Enterprise and Edu, an administrator must enable Luna first. Update workspace defaults, saved model settings, managed configurations, custom agents, and scheduled tasks with an available replacement. The `gpt-5.2` and `gpt-5.3-codex` models are already deprecated in Codex when you sign in with ChatGPT. Update scripts, configuration files, and `codex exec --model` commands that still reference those models. The OpenAI API and Codex authenticated with your own API key aren't affected by the GPT-5.4 retirement. For current API model availability, see the [API models page](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models). ## Configure your default local model The ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, and IDE extension use the same `config.toml` [configuration file](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/config-file/config-basic). To specify a model, add a `model` entry to your configuration file. If you don't specify a model, the ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, or IDE extension uses a recommended model. This example selects Sol in the app or CLI. When sharing a configuration with the IDE extension, pick a model available in every client you use, such as `gpt-6.1-sol`. ```toml model = "gpt-6.2-sol" ```
